books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, B. The American System and Sectionalism
Henry Clay and the American System

stimulus.text:
| Part of the plan | What it would do |
|---|---|---|
| Protective tariff | Tax imported goods so American-made goods cost less |
| Second Bank of the United States | Steady the currency and lend credit for business |
| Internal improvements | Build roads and canals to link the regions |

Henry Clay of Kentucky called the three parts his American System. Congress chartered the Second Bank and passed a protective tariff in 1816.

stem: Southern planters generally opposed the protective tariff in Clay’s plan because

options.text: it lowered the price of cotton in British markets
options.misconception: The tariff taxed imports into the United States; it did not set the price of cotton in Britain.

options.text: it forced the South to build factories of its own in every state
options.misconception: Nothing in the tariff forced anyone to build a factory; it only taxed imports.

options.text: it raised what they paid for manufactured goods while doing nothing for cotton exports
it ended the South’s trade with Britain entirely
options.misconception: Southern trade with Britain continued; the tariff made imports costlier, it did not end trade.

rationales.A: A tax on goods entering the United States does not set the price of cotton sold in Britain. The harm to planters was on what they bought, not what they sold.
rationales.B: The tariff made imported goods costlier so American goods looked cheaper. It built no factories and forced no region to build them.
rationales.C: Planters exported cotton and imported nearly everything they used. A protective tariff raised what they paid and gave their exports nothing back, so they called it sectional robbery.
rationales.D: Trade with Britain went on through the whole period. The tariff raised prices; it never stopped ships from sailing.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what a protective tariff does. It taxes imported goods so home-made goods cost less by comparison.
2. Ask who buys imports. Southern planters bought British cloth, tools, and goods, and sold cotton abroad.
3. Ask who gains. Northern manufacturers gain protection; planters gain nothing and pay more.
4. Put it together. The tariff taxed one region’s shopping to help another region’s factories.
Background: the South exported raw cotton to Britain and imported manufactured goods, so a tariff on imports fell hardest on Southern buyers.
Remember: to judge a tax, ask who pays it and who gains from it.
